cards.source_text: Wildfires in Indonesia are sweeping through a critical research site for Bornean orangutans and are now threatening a celebrated research camp, home to one of the world’s longest-running studies of wild apes. In the past few days, the fires have burned within 200 metres of Rangkong research station, a satellite of Cabang Panti research station, which lies about four miles north in Gunung Palung national park. Hundreds of Bornean orangutans (Pongo pygmaeus), one of three orangutan species, live in the direct vicinity of the research stations, with more than 2,500 thought to inhabit the park, many areas of which are now on fire. All three orangutan species are considered critically endangered. “Orangutans are fleeing from these forests. It’s just horrible,” said Prof Cheryl Knott, a biological anthropologist at Boston University who has been leading scientific research on orangutans at Cabang Panti for 32 years. In most cases, the fires were intentionally set to clear land, as is done every year on the island. But an extremely strong El Niño – a warming of sea-surface temperatures in the equatorial Pacific Ocean that disrupts global weather patterns – has fuelled exceptionally hot and dry conditions across the country, with fires easily escaping control as a result. In West Kalimantan province, some areas have gone months with little to no rainfall. Scientists at Cabang Panti have collected decades’ worth of data on wild orangutans and their life histories, following some of the same individuals from birth to grandmotherhood. Research carried out at the site has helped to establish the orangutan reproduction cycle, finding that the apes only give birth once every eight years – the longest cycle of any mammal. “The long-term nature of this database and the detailed nature of the database is unparalleled,” Knott said. But the fires threaten to undo such continuous observations. At the rate the flames are moving, without intervention or large firebreaks, the fires will reach Cabang Panti in 20 days’ time, scientists said. “[Cabang Panti] protects what has been, until now, one of the only truly ecologically intact tracts of lowland tropical rainforest in Borneo,” said Prof Andrew Marshall, an anthropologist at the University of Michigan who ran an ecological research project at the site from 2000 to 2020. “Without long-term, continuously collected field data, we cannot understand how tropical ecosystems are adapting to or suffering from global climate shifts.” I

cards.source_text: For the first time in the modern history of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), a Congolese nongovernmental organization will co-manage a protected area in the country. “It is an honor,” Dominique Bikaba, founder of the NGO Strong Roots, told Mongabay by phone. Strong Roots has been entrusted with the management of Itombwe Nature Reserve (RNI), located in South Kivu province in the northeast DRC. Under a public-private partnership Strong Roots will manage the reserve for the next 10 years. The Congolese Wildlife Authority (ICCN), the national authority responsible for natural parks, will retain oversight of the park. “I think the government chose us, because they have observed the work we have done in the biodiversity corridor and the way we have put local communities at the center of conservation,” Bikaba said. Strong Roots has spent about a decade securing land for communities and wildlife to create a 1-million-hectare (2.5-million-acre) corridor through community forestry concessions. This corridor spans the area between Kahuzi-Biega National Park and Itombwe Nature Reserve. To date, Strong Roots has secured 23 community forest concessions in the area, covering nearly 600,000 hectares (1.5 million acres) of land. “Itombwe is made up of seven chiefdoms, and we are already working with four of them in the corridor,” Bikaba said. “So we have a very good knowledge of the reserve; we know its problems and its needs.” Bikaba is a member of an Indigenous community in the area that was evicted to make way for another protected area. So, putting local populations at the center of conservation is particularly close to his heart, he said. Most protected areas in the DRC were created by evicting Indigenous populations, resulting in conflicts between park personnel and the local communities. Richard Fox, head of science at Butterfly Conservation, said: “Adult butterflies love hot, sunny weather for flying, feeding and breeding, and that’s exactly why people saw so many this summer. cards.source_text: It’s an ungainly word for English speakers, which is maybe why we do not hear it often: Gleichschaltung. Yet the concept remains central for a clear view of what happened to Germany in the 1930s. In 1933, the nation completely transformed, seemingly overnight, through “a concerted policy of ‘coordination’ (Gleichschaltung),” the U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum writes. “Culture, the economy, education, and law all came under Nazi control.” Those artists and organizations that were not purged had their essential character changed to reflect an entirely different set of artistic and political values. One publication, especially, serves as an example of the Nazification of culture. The arts journal Jugend (Youth), writes Messy Nessy Chic, “had been turned largely into propaganda” between 1933 and 1940, its final year. But prior to the regime’s takeover, Jugend showcased the most avant-garde, “degenerate” artists of the era, and might have been “the ‘brainiest’ periodical of the day,” as one critic wrote in a 1904 issue of The Yale Literary Magazine. “There is no magazine published in England or in this country which is at all like it.” You can take a look yourself—browse, search, and download hundreds of scanned issues of Jugend at the University of Heidelberg’s digital archive, thousands of pages in PDF form, spanning the magazine’s forty-four-year history. You can also see images at Flickr. As in England, France, Austria, and the U.S., the Art Nouveau movement in Germany emerged from a whirlwind of post-Impressionist painting, Orientalist motifs, folk art, modernist art and advertising, book illustration, and graphic and industrial design. Appropriately, given its perch on the threshold of a new century, Art Nouveau looked both backward—to the medieval, gothic, and Romantic—and forward toward a more modernist, urbane, and urbanized sensibility. So influential was Jugend that Art Nouveau in Germany became known as Jugendstil. The Oxford Critical and Cultural History of Modernist Magazines writes, “Among Jugend’s most important qualities—indeed, an essential aspect of Art Nouveau and its German equivalent Jugendstil—was its brilliant escapism.” Founded in 1896 by writer Georg Hirth, the magazine was “from the start a venue to promote the new cultural Renaissance without recourse to the established ‘vintage’ art.” (See its very first cover right above.) Jugendstil was primarily based in Munich, where most of its artists, designers, and writers lived and worked,

cards.source_text: Frank Lloyd Wright was often strapped for cash. In that respect, he had something in common with Vincent van Gogh, who passed most of his much shorter life in more dire circumstances. Unlike Wright, who enjoyed decades of fame at the pinnacle of the American architectural profession, van Gogh remained practically unknown until after his death. But if they’ve encountered one another in the afterlife, they’ve certainly discussed one subject above all others: their shared appreciation for Japanese woodblock prints. Here on Open Culture, we’ve previously featured the collection of 500 such works of art that van Gogh left behind. At the end of Wright’s life in 1959, he owned about 6,000, many of which his estate had to sell to pay both Japanese art dealers and American tax collectors. We could say that Wright died as he lived, advanced age having not evidently diminished either his financial recklessness or his obsession with ukiyo‑e. The masters of that classical “art of the floating world” like Hokusai and Hiroshige were among his favorite artists of any kind. When still a teenager, Wright went to work for the architect Joseph Silsbee, who’d built a chapel for his uncle. “Silsbee’s cousin, Ernest Fenollosa, happened to be the world’s leading Western expert on Japanese art at the time,” writes Kevin Nute at The Conversation. It isn’t certain how well the young Wright knew Fenollosa — or indeed when he began collecting ukiyo‑e, writes Frank Lloyd Wright and the Art of Japan author Julia Meech-Pekarik, though he may have seen both Hokusai and Hiroshige’s works at the World’s Columbian Exposition in Chicago in 1893, “about the time he opened his practice in Oak Park.” Eight years later, “Wright made his first voyage to Japan in pursuit of prints, and he did indeed return with enough expertise to stage an exhibition of his own Hiroshige collection at the Art Institute of Chicago in March of 1906.” He returned for two months in 1913, making it clear that he was only interested in using that time to acquire more prints. Later, while working on the Imperial Hotel between 1917 and 1922, he spent a total of more than three years there, later writing that “the pursuit of the Japanese print became my constant recreation while in Tokio,” a quest whose “adventures and excursions would take place at night or sometimes call for a journey by day to distant places.” This positioned him well to take on a sideline as a dealer (or as he liked to call himself, a merchant) of Japan

cards.source_text: Deep into the night, and out of our sight, tiny claws rake over plastic. The animal skitters halfway through a pipe, then stops. A hunter five times its weight is on its tail, but it is safe from harm, and not just because the tunnel is too narrow for the hunter to enter. Curiosity killed the cat’s predatory thoughts with a face full of prickles a long time ago. The cat sniffs the tube, and wanders off. Until this summer, we had never laid eyes on our hedgehogs, not once in two years. Moist poos glistening with beetle shells told us they were here. But lawns like crispy seaweed, beds full of papered flowers, and reports of dehydrated waifs made us worried for them. Water baths slaked a thirst, but where were the invertebrates, the crunch of a carapace, a slug smoothie? A reputable website advised us to feed hedgehogs cat food and beetles. We have six cats using our garden as their public convenience – should it be their takeaway too? As for the beetles, if an insectivorous mammal can’t find any, how could we? At the beginning of August, our car left a DIY store looking equipped for a motorised joust, with a three-metre lance (aka drainpipe) thrust out of the front passenger window. Every night since, dinner has been served in a foil tray, down the pipe, cut to a third of its length but still beyond cat reach. Every morning, the tray is found nudged out the other end, empty. Our trail camera has captured all this, giving us Somerset’s answer to the snow leopard, live action photos of the otherwise unseen. It has recorded entrances and exits, both to the food pipe and the garden itself, slipping between slats at the front, or slotting through the purpose‑made hog hole in the fence at the back. And here the comedy ends. We’ll stop this supplementary feeding in time for hibernation, but how will hedgehogs fare next summer and in summers to come? Must we manage the emergency for as long as it takes them to adapt and evolve? Will they?
cards.source_title: Country diary: Drama on the trail cam – this is Somerset’s version of the snow leopard | Derek Niemann

cards.source_text: The British-American novelist, playwright and commentator Bonnie Greer has died aged 77. In a statement, her husband David Hutchins said that she died on Tuesday evening following a brief illness. Greer’s “intelligence, courage and distinctive voice made an enduring contribution to British cultural and public life”, said Hutchins. “To me, she was my partner, confidante and inspiration, and I feel profoundly privileged to have shared my life with her.” Born on 16 November 1948, Greer moved from the US to the UK in 1986, and became a citizen in 1997. Greer’s work – which often focused on the lives of minorities, and of women – spanned novels, nonfiction, plays and broadcasting. Her first book, Hanging By Her Teeth, published in 1994, was a novel about a Black American woman travelling through the US and Europe in search of her father. Her later books included Obama Music (2009), about her and the former US president’s connections to Chicago’s South Side, and Langston Hughes: The Value of Contradiction (2011), a biography of the Harlem Renaissance figure. In 2022, she was made a fellow of the Royal Society of Literature. Greer regularly appeared as a panellist on Newsnight Review and Question Time. She served on the boards of the Royal Opera House, the British Museum and the London Film School, and was chancellor of Kingston University, London. In the 2010 birthday honours, she was appointed OBE for contribution to the arts. Hutchins said that “those closest to Bonnie will remember her warmth, humour, generosity and extraordinary ability to bring people together”. More to follow
cards.source_title: Bonnie Greer, writer and cultural commentator, dies aged 77

cards.source_text: Ben Macintyre uses the acronym MICE to describe the reasons people betray their countries: Money, Ideology, Coercion or Ego. In the set-piece that opens his latest work of true-espionage, we discover a new reason: erectile dysfunction. Stressed, drinking too much, under constant surveillance, furious about the corruption of his colleagues and frustrated with his home life, the KGB’s Vladimir Kuzichkin is offering to betray the secrets of his homeland and its Iranian allies, if only a British doctor can help him have sex again. If you have read Macintyre before, you’ll recognise a classic example of his style: the journalist’s eye for salacious detail combined with a historian’s rigour. The rest of Redwood lives up to the attention-grabbing opening scene; I devoured it in a single sitting. If you haven’t read him, he is the author of a hatful of bestselling books about war, politics and secrecy, several of which have been adapted for the screen, and one of which – Operation Mincemeat – has become a West End and Broadway musical. They are sometimes derided as “dadlit”, the kind of nonfiction read by golf club bores and armchair colonels. But Redwood is as far above yet-another-book-about-the-second-world-war as a George Smiley novel is above Jack Reacher. The setting is the immediate aftermath of the 1979 revolution that brought Iran’s ayatollahs to power. The west was on the back foot, having lost a key ally, with the Americans particularly discomfited by Islamists having seized their embassy and taken its staff hostage. The Soviets, meanwhile, thought they had an opportunity to spread their influence south, to a strategic and oil-rich country with warm water ports. Kuzichkin’s job was to further this aim by distributing money, arms and encouragement to the Tudeh party, an orthodox communist movement led by a Stalinist who had spent the previous few decades in exile in East Germany. He ran his operation out of the huge Soviet embassy, where his mostly useless colleagues celebrated even the smallest of successes with vast quantities of vodka, and he really hated it. Literally across the street, in the equally large British embassy, was Ian McCredie, a young MI6 operative who had recently arrived in Tehran with a wife and baby in tow, his task to re-establish a British intelligence presence after the entire team had been forced to leave. He didn’t drink as much as Kuzichkin, but he did discover 50 crates of whisky that a predecessor had imported as a present
cards.source_title: Redwood by Ben Macintyre review – a superbly wrought tale of cold war defection

This intimately told sophomore novel, again a story of friendship, precarity and community, is at once an elegy, a spoken-word poem and a journalistic meditation, repeatedly asking readers: “So, are you listening?” For our unnamed narrator, “hurts come in different shapes each time”: from the childhood scars of her father’s abandonment, to sexism in the creative scene and the difficulties of navigating short-lived flatshares on universal credit (“If you don’t know about being money dry, if you don’t know loss – you don’t get it. If you know, you know”). Her journey of personal discovery is mapped on to the contemporary travails of London’s wider working-class inner-city diaspora communities as she calculates her life by doorways, “walking past each one” without a roadmap for her personal and professional goals. At the centre of the novel is the loss of the narrator’s closest confidante, referred to as “My Favourite Person”. As his untimely death becomes fodder for gossip, she addresses those questioning how he died: “You’re asking for information but to me it’s the loop, the scaffolding, never comes down, this con of process, all dying to know how he died.” Meanwhile, she remembers their late-night phone calls, continues to leave him unheard voicemails: “Don’t want to do it all without you on my team.” How to survive in a world darkened by an unshakeable loss? “Memories are a bit like a messy laundry cupboard. cards.source_text: In some rare cases, adaptations and interpretations of a literary work can surpass the source. Despite hundreds of valiant efforts on the part of fans, filmmakers, game/toy designers, and radio producers, this has never been true of the fully-realized fantasy world in J.R.R. Tolkien’s The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings trilogy (not that it’s ever been anyone’s intent). As we noted in a previous post, Tolkien’s fictional world is so intricate, its sources so vast and varied, that Corey Olsen, “The Tolkien Professor,” has made it his entire life’s work to open that world up to students and curious readers, such as with his eight-part lecture series on The Hobbit. One might also add illustrators to the list of Tolkien interpreters above who have—in the almost ninety years since The Hobbit’s publication and more than seventy years since the first appearance of The Lord of the Rings trilogy—done their best to visualize Tolkien’s world. But perhaps no one did so better than the master himself. Long known as a visual artist as well as a literary one, Tolkien left behind over 100 illustrations for The Hobbit, one of which adorns 2011’s HarperCollins 75th anniversary edition of the book. He also created these original cover designs for each book in The Lord of the Rings trilogy. In the long and complex publication history of Tolkien’s most famous of works, it’s unclear if these designs ever made it onto books published during his lifetime, but the sigil in the center of The Fellowship of the Ring design (above), with its ominous eye of Sauron surrounded by elvish runes and topped by the one ring, did grace the elegant, minimalist covers of the first edition of the trilogy. Tolkien’s artwork received a thorough treatment in a 1995 monograph J.R.R. Tolkien Artist & Illustrator, which covers over 60 years of Tolkien’s life as an artist, and the magic of flickr brings us this compendium of Tolkien illustrations. Note: An earlier version of this post appeared on our site in 2013. cards.source_text: Humans have prized marble for its colours, patterns, texture and heft for thousands of years. In this video, Mary McGillivray, a digital creator and PhD student at the University of Melbourne, explores how, for as long as we’ve prized it, we’ve been inventing ways to fake it. McGillivray traverses Europe to investigate how, from ancient Rome to modern home-improvement stores, we’ve developed techniques to cast, plaster and paint imitations of the metamorphic rock. And, as McGillivray argues, this process has been about more than finding a cheap alternative to a luxury material. Rather, the millennia-long history of our fascination with marble, and of our attempts to recreate it, has much to say about how humanity is inspired by, and competes with, the natural world. cards.source_text: When he was a child growing up in Emilia-Romagna, my great-grandfather Marco once found an eagle fledgling that had fallen from its nest. He kept it warm in the folds of his shirt and ran home, only to discover as he undressed that the bird had eaten strips of his flesh, its beak tinged red with blood. The rescued eagle thrived in my great-grandfather’s care, its wingspan soon a remarkable length. And all the while, Marco himself grew immensely tall. Then, one day, without warning, the eagle flew away. The moment my father told me this story when I was a boy, it lodged itself deep in my imagination. I pictured young Marco as a giant striding through the forests of north-central Italy, calling to the bird of prey, waiting in vain for it to land on his outstretched hand. Marco merged with the heroes of my illustrated classical civilisation books, earning his place between the busts of Roman emperors and the chapters on Greek mythology. What I never realised was that this family legend held clues to who I am and to my relationship to Italy. Lina Stores deli in Soho, London, has been a pillar of Italian life in England for decades. It’s where we’d sometimes meet our paternal grandparents when visiting London from our home in France. My brothers and I would line up in front of the refrigerated counter and ask for our favourite ravioli, doing our utmost to avoid any slip-ups in Italian that would make the staff wince: ‘ricotta e spinaci’, ‘zucca’, ‘funghi porcini’. Back at our grandparents’ flat, Nonna served the ravioli on an elaborately laid table, and my grandfather appeared with freshly grated Parmigiano. He’d sprinkle the cheese evenly over our pasta; never too much, nor too little. How he did this, and with such speed, we didn’t know. If we had spaghetti, Nonna would wrap her right hand around ours and twirl the fork with us so we held just the right amount, the bespattered tablecloth damning proof of our slapdash habits at home. My grandparents trusted that these rituals of the table (they saw them as basic codes of Italianness, connecting displaced Italians everywhere) would allow us to paper over the differences in our ethnically blended and peripatetic family. In this way, we’d be able to claim Italian identity for ourselves, despite its competition in our lives with Englishness and Frenchness. cards.source_text: ‘What do you think this movie is about?’ In this video essay, the US filmmaker Kevin B Lee recalls the shock of seeing, as a young film buff, the raw, violent and widely acclaimed Vietnam War film Platoon (1986) with his family in a San Francisco cinema. Recording outside the building that once housed that cinema, he details his harrowing time in the theatre and the film’s reverberations in his life beyond the theatre’s walls, including how it stirred generational trauma in his family and racism at school. With his deceptively simple approach, Lee inverts and subverts Oliver Stone’s epic, crafting, on a shoestring budget, a profound and intensely personal meditation on memory. Lee’s video essay was published as part of ‘Once Upon a Screen’, a series of video essays about film viewing and childhood trauma, commissioned and curated by Ariel Avissar and Evelyn Kreutzer, for The Cine-Files journal of cinema studies, Issue 15.

cards.source_text: Owen Williams wrote the last Tubs album, Cotton Crown, in the midst of a breakdown. But the harder you squint at their catalog, the harder it is to surmise what is breakdown and what is not. The Welsh singer’s unreliable narrators slip between gurning heartache and a self-sniping internal monologue that says cruel things you would never accept from a friend. His trade is failure anthems set to jangly folk-rock that stops short of storming the barn. Their darkest snapshots of tragedy and depression are often their funniest and winningest. On “Heaven or London” from their new record, Hard Life, Williams portrays himself as “the singer of a rip-off band” who is “wanking himself into an early grave,” playing “farm simulator,” and, for some reason, claiming to “write for The New York Times.” There is no tried-and-true path to success for a man like this, and it is unclear if Williams would take it. “I don’t wanna sell out this tour,” sings another of his narrators over duelling guitar and fiddle. “Don’t wanna play with the Tubs anymore/If you don’t love me.” The Tubs are the sort of band that has been down on its luck for so long that “down with luck” becomes its manifesto. The only thing for it is a crack at the small time: Write and record quickly, play gazillions of gigs, amble over to America, maybe briefly become the talk of the town. It helps to sign to one of the bigger indies; the new album is their Merge debut. But the uncertain journey ahead will be subject to chance, as well as a pathological fidelity to indie-pop principles: the DIY stance, the affinity for ruin, and the belief that love can make it all worthwhile but, knowing your luck, probably won’t. No score yet, be the first to add. Like many oddball bands operating in London, the Tubs’ longing for a dirtier, scrappier version of the city dovetails with a distaste for music likely to make much money. It is hard to disentangle their romantic fatalism from their tech-ravaged industry and dire social conditions. The rewards of a rich artistic life come to those who remain open to the world, which can be hard when paying a fortune for a crap apartment well into your thirties. Money helps, as does delirious self-belief. The Tubs, like so many bloody-minded artists living 40 to 50 years too late, appear to have scant hope of either. The rest of the band, for all their ramshackle fervor, barely put up a fight against Williams’ defeatist lyrics. Lead guitarist Dan Lucas is new to the fold—George Nichol

cards.source_text: Haruomi Hosono has been at the vanguard of pop music for the majority of his nearly 60-year career. He spearheaded Japan’s folk-rock boom in the 1970s with Happy End, sparked the synth-pop revolution of the 1980s with Yellow Magic Orchestra, and has written for, performed on, or otherwise contributed to thousands of records. But recently, the 79-year-old artist has been looking in the rearview. In 2019, he circled back to his country-inspired 1973 solo debut, Hosono House, and reworked it into Hochono House, which somehow sounded even more retro than the original. “I was curious to see if I returned to these songs now and played them with my current feelings, what would happen?” he said. It seems that he’s still got unfinished business. Incomplete ideas continue to haunt Hosono like spirits in purgatory; on his 23rd solo album, Yours Sincerely, he puts them to a merciful rest. He has scoured the last couple decades of his catalog for rough gems in need of polishing, casting a wide net: music for film, television, and streaming video; commissions for department stores and clothing designers; even quixotic reimaginings of Liszt and Beethoven, making peace with the statue of Beethoven that sat in his grandfather’s room, scowling at him every day of his youth. The selection shows a more contemplative side to his craft rarely seen outside his freelance work, his tender heart exposed and beating in an unhurried waltz time. No score yet, be the first to add. Ghosts of Hosono’s past are all over Yours Sincerely. One, “Rojiura (Walking Vibration),” is salvaged from a sparse instrumental he composed for the 2006 NHK drama Walkers: Maigo no Otonatachi, its snappy percussion now augmented with traditional iwabue flute and Hosono’s soft crooning. He gives an even more dramatic retooling to “Happy Holiday,” expanded from a short jingle for department store Parco’s 2024 holiday advertisements into an exuberant flurry of clamoring bells and electronically processed vocal harmonies. (“I’m not using any of that trendy AI technology,” he stresses in the production notes.) cards.source_text: Seconds into her debut mixtape, Karrahbooo steps out of the spotlight. “I don’t want to link, I stay out the way,” she explains on “Inside the Booth,” tone unphased enough to back it up. It’s a pretty diplomatic opening for an artist who has spent the past two years fighting her way off the bench. After emerging as one to watch in Lil Yachty’s Concrete Boys collective, Karrahboo cut ties with the crew amid a public label dispute that left her estranged from Yachty and unable to drop for two years. (Yachty has refuted claims that he held back her music.) Out of that limbo arises NOT DA 2, a set of low-stakes trap and plugg cuts too collected to convey frustration. Karrahbooo first blew up thanks to a formidable showing on a 2024 On the Radar crew cypher. Flanked by a summer camp cabin’s worth of Concrete Boys jockeying for the mic, her dark gaze and blunt bars exerted a slick authority. Karrahbooo’s composure distinguishes her from various peers and Future progeny like Anycia, whose baritone raps could be delivered between rose-wrapped blunt rips, or Veeze, whose voice all but drips with promethazine. She tends to come off more like Wednesday Addams taking over Camp Chippewa in Addams Family Values, clocking everyone from a mile away with a remove that’s less icy than detached. No score yet, be the first to add. Early single “No Hook” makes the strongest case for this ultra-nonchalant persona, and it only takes a minute. Playing out almost like a Rap Shit oner, the song tracks KB through a night of pit stops and party fouls over Halloween B-movie synth—thank God her driver lets her hotbox in the back. Somewhere between making sure the club owner knows she’s coming and her good-for-nothing man knows there’s “nothing to discuss,” she fires off direct-to-camera disses formatted like advice. A bouncer is “doing a lot for a job that’s not paying enough”; a girl with a problem “should confront me, you don’t want to keep it pent up.” Karrahbooo may be pro-airing it out, but NOT DA 2 is pretty muted. cards.source_text: It’s easy to forget—especially today—that being retro can actually mean being modern. Retro styles let artists treat history like a patchwork: transmuting an homage into something new, using the past to tell stories of the present, creating today out of yesterday. Denshattack!, the new rhythmic trick-based platformer from indie developer Undercoders, reads from Y2K Sega like it’s the Bible. The game has the beaming cell-shaded graphics of Jet Set Radio, the high-octane attitude of 3D-era Sonic the Hedgehog, and the hedonistic gameplay of Crazy Taxi. But Denshattack! parlays its old scripture into a product of the now—not even cracked-out late-’90s Sega could make a game where you perform skateboarding tricks as subway trains in the name of fighting climate change and AI. New matters, old styles; 1999, meet 2026. But even with all of this retro glory, Denshattack! would be an abject failure if it didn’t get its music right. Gaming soundtracks at the turn of the millennium spanned futurist dance, funk, hip-hop, and hard-rocking pop; these sounds are arguably the games’ most widely-known feature, their influence scattered across new albums and Instagram Reels alike. Denshattack!’s cocktail of these sounds is the best and most ambitious aspect of its perfect sense of retro. Featuring an all-star team of composers from video games’ past, present, and future, Denshattack!’s 80-track score adds a shining original product to the ongoing continuum of Y2K gaming. No score yet, be the first to add. Rising video game composers deploy new forms of old styles up and down the tracklist. Andrew One’s back-to-back tracks “Glow Up!” and “I Like the Way” feel like funky Dreamcast scores in an updated make and model, the latter featuring the classy attitude of the Metropolis Street Racer soundtrack with 2020s K-pop vocals replacing its ’90s R&B. cards.source_text: Maybe it’s dumb to be a believer. There’s no guarantee that your beliefs will hold up, and it’s unlikely the thing you reach out for will ever reach back. But to commit to this possibility, as Angela Autumn figures it, is to find connection: to the universe, to other people, or to God if you’re lucky. “I got to be a believer to take a ride,” she sings on the title track of her third studio album, Believer. The people on Autumn’s album have faith in lovers who may not return, in money, in fame, and in nature as a refuge. Autumn herself has had to believe in her songs through an increasingly unstable music economy, moving from a book-your-own-shows independent musician toward a more formal recording career, while also moving further from the sturdy framework of meaning she grew up with. The album is about what belief can engender when certainty is gone, and the possibility of transforming that which is old and battered into something new. No score yet, be the first to add. Autumn grew up Catholic outside Pittsburgh, in the Allegheny region she calls the “Paris of Appalachia.” She was raised around music and nature: Her mother played didgeridoo and made instruments from gourds; her father and family sang together in church. She began playing guitar and banjo at 19, and mainly plays the latter these days, borrowing its open tuning and clawhammer playing style; she also tends to play in an irregular structure indebted to Appalachian music. Influenced by contemporary roots musicians including Rhiannon Giddens, Allison Russell, and Gillian Welch, Autumn eventually moved to Nashville, writing songs that moved between country, indie rock, and grungegrass. She has an anti-purist and anti-revivalist approach to the traditions of Appalachia, but a great reverence for it all the same. Her voice is her music’s most recognizable “Appalachian” element: high, pinched, effortful; sometimes it sounds as if a sneeze could sing, elsewhere gravelly as a cough from a harsh hookah drag. Autumn wrote Believer in isolation, in a treehouse outside Asheville, as well as in the Tennessee woods and in an empty warehouse near Chattanooga. Across the record, the physical world—the Blue Ridge mountains, woods, streams, changing weather—is where her songs go when human relationships become untenable. items.summary: This story of Soviet agent and his MI6 handler in revolutionary Iran is a page-turning masterpiece Ben Macintyre uses the acronym MICE to describe the reasons people betray their countries: Money, Ideology, Coercion or Ego. Stressed, drinking too much, under constant surveillance, furious about the corruption of his colleagues and frustrated with his home life, the KGB’s Vladimir Kuzichkin is offering to betray the secrets of his homeland and its Iranian allies, if only a British doctor can help him have sex again. items.title: Safe Spaces by Tice Cin review – a kaleidoscopic vision of precarity, music and grief
items.summary: Part spoken-word poem, part journalistic meditation, this is an inventive, tender novel of a songwriter’s journey through love and loss in London Tice Cin’s philosophical and poetic new novel about a young Turkish-Cypriot songwriter and music producer extends the preoccupations of her prizewinning debut, 2021’s Keeping the House . This intimately told sophomore novel, again a story of friendship, precarity and community, is at once an elegy, a spoken-word poem and a journalistic meditation, repeatedly asking readers: “So, are you listening?” For our unnamed narrator, “hurts come in different shapes each time”: from the childhood scars of her father’s abandonment, to sexism in the creative scene and the difficulties of navigating short-lived flatshares on universal credit (“If you don’t know about being money dry, if you don’t know loss – you don’t get it. If you know, you know”). Her journey of personal discovery is mapped on to the contemporary travails of London’s wider working-class inner-city diaspora communities as she calculates her life by doorways, “walking past each one” without a roadmap for her personal and professional goals.
